cases.presenting_complaint: Third episode of depression - low mood, social withdrawal, and sleep problems for 2 months
cases.associated: Difficulty getting out of bed, reduced work performance, conflict with husband over household responsibilities, intermittent crying spells, passive death wishes
cases.risk_factors: Two previous episodes (age 22 and 29), family history of depression (mother and maternal aunt), discontinuation of maintenance antidepressant 6 months ago, current life stressors
cases.mse: Appearance: Appropriately dressed, appears tired. Behavior: Slow movements, reluctant to engage. Speech: Reduced rate, soft volume. Mood: 'Everything is falling apart again'. Affect: Depressed, flat, tearful. Thought: Hopelessness about recurrence, negative self-evaluation, passive death wishes. Perception: No abnormality. Cognition: Preserved but reports poor concentration. Insight: Good - recognizes depression
cases.investigations: Blood: TSH normal, B12 normal, no recent substance use. PHQ-9: 20/27 (moderately severe). Previous records confirm diagnosis and treatment response
cases.suicide_risk: Moderate risk. Passive suicidal ideation, history of recurrence, recent medication discontinuation. Protective factors: treatment adherence previously, supportive husband, children
cases.explanation: This represents recurrent Major Depressive Disorder (3rd episode). Recurrence rates are high - approximately 50% after one episode, increasing with each recurrence. Discontinuation of maintenance antidepressant is a significant precipitant. Past treatment response (if documented) predicts future response. The patient has insight and can participate in treatment decisions. Recurrence prevention is crucial - maintenance antidepressant for at least 2 years, possibly longer given 3 episodes
cases.management: (1) Restart antidepressant - preferably same medication that worked previously (if known); (2) Discuss importance of maintenance treatment - at least 2 years, potentially lifelong given 3 episodes; (3) Psychosocial interventions: CBT to prevent relapse, interpersonal therapy; (4) Address precipitants: discuss with husband about分担 household stress; (5) Monitor for suicidality weekly initially; (6) Consider psychotherapy augmentation; (7) If poor response, consider augmentation with lithium or atypical antipsychotic; (8) Develop crisis plan; (9) Family psychoeducation; (10) Regular follow-up for at least 2 years

cases.presenting_complaint: Longstanding low energy, oversleeping, and carb craving despite appearing 'fine' to others
cases.associated: Sleeping 10-14 hours daily still unrefreshed, 8kg weight gain, intense carbohydrate craving (especially sweets and rice), leaden paralysis (heavy arms and legs in morning), hypersensitive to rejection causing relationship difficulties, anhedonia, mood reactivity (improves temporarily with positive events)
cases.risk_factors: Family history of mood disorders (uncle with bipolar), introvert personality, sedentary lifestyle, social media use pattern affecting sleep
cases.mse: Appearance: Overweight, casual dress. Behavior: Slow to respond, appears fatigued. Speech: Normal rate, somewhat drawling. Mood: 'Heavy and sluggish'. Affect: Mildly depressed, mood-reactive during positive discussion. Thought: No psychosis, rejects criticism sensitively. Perception: No abnormality. Cognition: Mild concentration issues, memory intact. Insight: Partial - recognizes he's different but not depressed
cases.investigations: Blood: TSH 4.5 (borderline high, repeat needed), fasting glucose 6.2 (impaired), lipid profile shows elevated triglycerides. PHQ-9: 12/27. Sleep study: Excessive daytime sleepiness, no apnea
cases.suicide_risk: Low risk. No suicidal ideation, though reports sometimes wishing he could 'just sleep forever'. Good social support, religious faith
cases.explanation: Atypical depression is characterized by mood reactivity plus at least 2 of: leaden paralysis, hypersomnia, appetite/weight gain, and sensitivity to rejection. More common in younger adults, females, and those with earlier onset. Often chronic course. Borderline TSH warrants monitoring for subclinical hypothyroidism which can present similarly. Carb craving and leaden paralysis are hallmark features distinguishing it from typical/melancholic depression
cases.management: (1) Repeat TSH in 6 weeks; (2) MAO-Is are most effective for atypical depression but dietary restrictions and drug interactions limit use; SSRIs are alternative first-line; (3) Behavioral activation - gradual increase in activity despite leaden paralysis; (4) Regular sleep schedule (not oversleeping); (5) Address carbohydrate cravings through balanced diet; (6) Interpersonal psychotherapy; (7) Gradual exercise program; (8) Address sensitivity to rejection in therapy; (9) Monitor weight and metabolic parameters; (10) Phototherapy if seasonal component suspected; (11) Psychoeducation about atypical features

cases.presenting_complaint: Three-week history of low mood, decreased need for sleep, and increased productivity at work
cases.associated: Decreased sleep without fatigue, rapid speech, racing thoughts, spending sprees (bought three phones), increased goal-directed activity, grandiose beliefs about investment abilities, previous similar episode 2 years ago treated as 'stress'
cases.risk_factors: Family history of bipolar disorder (maternal cousin), previous episode misdiagnosed, recent work promotion stress, sleep deprivation
cases.mse: Appearance: Well-dressed, energetic. Behavior: Restless, fidgety, pressured to leave for 'business meetings'. Speech: Pressured, increased rate and volume. Mood: 'Great, I've never felt better!'. Affect: Expansive, irritable when interrupted. Thought: Flight of ideas, grandiosity (claims he will make millions), no true delusions. Perception: No hallucinations. Cognition: Distractible, insight impaired regarding illness
cases.investigations: Blood: TSH normal, electrolytes normal, drug screen negative. Young Mania Rating Scale (YMRS): 22 (moderate mania). Previous episode history suggests bipolar diagnosis
cases.suicide_risk: Moderate risk during depression phase, low during mania. Current phase is mixed with elevated mood and depression symptoms concurrently. Risk of impulsivity during mania with spending/sex
cases.explanation: This presentation represents Bipolar Depression, likely Bipolar I given history of previous manic/hypomanic episode. The current episode shows mixed features - elevated mood, decreased sleep, grandiosity (manic symptoms) alongside 3-week low mood period. This could represent: (1) Antidepressant-induced switch, (2) Natural cycling, or (3) Mixed episode. Important to distinguish from unipolar depression as antidepressants alone can worsen bipolar. Previous episode at age 30 was likely hypomania or mania misdiagnosed
cases.management: (1) URGENT: Mood stabilizer initiation required - lithium or valproate first-line; (2) Avoid antidepressants as monotherapy (risk of switching to mania); (3) If manic symptoms predominate, consider atypical antipsychotic (quetiapine, olanzapine, aripiprazole); (4) Admit if severe mania or safety concerns; (5) Psychoeducation about bipolar disorder; (6) Sleep hygiene critical (sleep deprivation worsens cycling); (7) Avoid alcohol and recreational drugs; (8) Regular mood monitoring; (9) Family involvement; (10) Long-term mood stabilizer for prevention; (11) Work with employer regarding time off; (12) Crisis plan for future episodes

cases.presenting_complaint: Profound depression with inability to feel any pleasure, early morning wakening, and severe psychomotor disturbance for 4 weeks
cases.associated: Complete anhedonia (no pleasure from family, food, or previously enjoyed activities), terminal insomnia (wakes 4am daily), marked psychomotor retardation (spends most day in bed), severe anorexia with 7kg weight loss, profound guilt about past sins, feels he deserves punishment, non-reactive mood (nothing improves his state)
cases.risk_factors: Retired army officer, rigid personality, first depressive episode, recent retirement 8 months ago, loss of identity and purpose
cases.mse: Appearance: Markedly cachectic, neglected hygiene, looks much older. Behavior: Marked psychomotor retardation, requires assistance to walk, slow movements. Speech: Very slow, delayed responses, minimal spontaneous speech. Mood: 'Empty, dead inside'. Affect: Flat, non-reactive. Thought: Excessive guilt, worthlessness, nihilistic delusions ('I'm already dead', 'My soul is damned'). Perception: No hallucinations. Cognition: Oriented but severely slowed. Insight: Partial - knows he's ill but feels deserving
cases.investigations: Blood: TSH normal, cortisol slightly elevated (likely stress response), B12 low-normal, folate low. PHQ-9: 26/27 (severe). HAM-D: 28 (very severe)
cases.suicide_risk: HIGH RISK. Severe guilt, nihilistic delusions, psychomotor retardation may make attempt less likely but risk is substantial. Requires close observation
cases.explanation: Melancholic depression is a severe subtype characterized by: anhedonia, non-reactive mood, psychomotor disturbance, terminal insomnia, excessive guilt, anorexia, and diurnal variation (worse morning). This patient meets all criteria. More common in older adults, males, and those with first-episode late-life depression. Associated with HPA axis dysregulation. Poor response to psychotherapy alone, requires biological treatment. Delusions of guilt/worthlessness suggest psychotic features (mood-congruent)
cases.management: (1) Admit to psychiatric unit given severity; (2) ECT is highly effective for melancholic depression - consider early given severity; (3) If medication preferred: start SSRI (e.g., sertraline 100mg) or SNRI; (4) High dose likely needed; (5) Augmentation with atypical antipsychotic if psychotic features; (6) Nutritional support; (7) Monitor physical health closely; (8) Family support and education; (9) Address identity loss from retirement; (10) Rehabilitation post-recovery; (11) Maintenance treatment given severity

cases.presenting_complaint: Severe depression with beliefs that she is 'already dead' and 'the devil has taken over her body' for 6 weeks
cases.associated: Profound psychomotor retardation, stopped eating believing body is 'not real', delusional guilt about past affair (actually minor emotional connection years ago), believes she deserves eternal punishment, refusing to speak to family, tactile hallucinations of 'demons touching her'
cases.risk_factors: First severe episode, recent discovery of husband's emotional affair 3 months ago, family history of psychosis in uncle (schizophrenia), early childhood trauma
cases.mse: Appearance: Disheveled, neglected, appears catatonic-like. Behavior: Very slow movements, mute at times. Speech: Minimal, when speaks says she is 'already gone'. Mood: 'Nothing, I'm dead'. Affect: Flat, inappropriate (smiles when discussing death). Thought: Delusions of guilt (exaggerated guilt about past affair), nihilistic delusions ('my body is dead'), somatic delusions, possible delusions of control (demons). Perception: Tactile hallucinations of demons touching her. Cognition: Severely impaired, disoriented to time. Insight: Poor - doesn't accept psychiatric illness
cases.investigations: Blood: TSH normal, electrolytes show mild hyponatremia (likely SIADH from depression), normal drug screen. CT head: Normal. PHQ-9: Cannot complete due to psychosis. CAMCOG: Impaired
cases.suicide_risk: HIGH RISK. Psychosis with nihilistic delusions, severe psychomotor retardation, refusal of nutrition. Combined risk of suicide, neglect, and medical complications
cases.explanation: Psychotic Depression is major depression with psychotic features (delusions or hallucinations). Prevalence 15-20% of major depression. Psychosis is mood-congruent (guilt, worthlessness, nihilism, punishment) or mood-incongruent. This case shows both: mood-congruent guilt delusions and mood-incongruent nihilistic/somatic delusions plus tactile hallucinations. High risk for suicide, neglect, and medical complications. Requires combination of antidepressant and antipsychotic, or ECT. Poor prognosis if untreated
cases.management: (1) ADMIT IMMEDIATELY - psychiatric unit with medical monitoring; (2) Combination therapy: antidepressant + antipsychotic (e.g., sertraline 100-200mg + quetiapine 100-300mg); (3) ECT is highly effective - consider if rapid response needed or medication fails; (4) Monitor nutrition and hydration; (5) Monitor sodium levels; (6) Address physical neglect; (7) Family meeting - explain condition; (8) Once stabilized, explore past trauma in psychotherapy; (9) Couple therapy may help if husband agreeable; (10) Long-term maintenance treatment; (11) Monitor for relapse

cases.diagnosis: Depression with Comorbid Borderline Personality Disorder
cases.presenting_complaint: Chronic feelings of emptiness, self-harm, and intense unstable relationships alongside depressive episodes
cases.duration: Depressive episode: 6 weeks. Underlying BPD: 5+ years
cases.associated: Current: Low mood, crying spells, passive suicidal ideation. Chronic BPD features: Self-harm (cutting arms), intense fear of abandonment, stormy relationships, identity disturbance ('don't know who I am'), chronic emptiness, affective instability (mood shifts within hours), transient paranoia under stress
cases.risk_factors: Childhood sexual abuse (disclosed at age 12), unstable attachment with alcoholic mother, multiple broken relationships, recent breakup with boyfriend, job instability, history of multiple suicide attempts (3)
cases.mse: Appearance: Multiple scars on forearms (healing), gothic-style dress. Behavior: Engages readily but mood shifts during interview. Speech: Variable rate, emotional. Mood: 'Empty, alone, worthless'. Affect: Labile - tearful, then angry, then flat. Thought: Passive SI, no active plan, splitting attitudes evident. Perception: No psychosis. Cognition: Insight variable. Insight: Partial - acknowledges emotional difficulties
cases.investigations: Blood: TSH normal, B12 normal. PHQ-9: 16/27. Personality assessment suggests BPD (SCID-II). No acute medical issues from cutting
cases.suicide_risk: HIGH RISK. History of multiple attempts, current self-harm, BPD features (impulsivity, emotional dysregulation). Requires careful assessment and close monitoring
cases.explanation: Comorbid depression and Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD) is common - 30-40% of BPD patients meet criteria for major depression. Distinguishing features: chronic emptiness (vs. episodic low mood), identity disturbance, abandonment fears, self-harm as emotion regulation (not suicidal intent), affective instability. Prognosis better than pure BPD when depression treated. BPD itself responds to specific therapies (DBT, MBT, TFP). Self-harm may decrease with effective treatment
cases.management: (1) Treat depression: SSRI (e.g., sertraline 50-100mg) - may help irritability and impulsivity; (2) URGENT: Refer for specialized BPD treatment - DBT (Dialectical Behavior Therapy) is gold standard; (3) Consider MBT or schema therapy as alternatives; (4) Ensure safety - contract for safety, crisis plan; (5) Reduce self-harm: DBT skills, identifying triggers, alternative behaviors; (6) Address attachment issues in therapy; (7) Pharmacotherapy for specific BPD symptoms (mood instability, anxiety); (8) Avoid hospitalization unless acute high risk; (9) Consistent, boundaried therapeutic relationship; (10) Coordinate care (psychologist + psychiatrist); (11) Family psychoeducation; (12) Long-term treatment - BPD improves over time with appropriate therapy

cases.diagnosis: Depression with Grief Complicated by Unresolved Conflict
cases.presenting_complaint: Persistent depression since husband's death 10 months ago, unable to 'move on' despite family pressure
cases.associated: Intense yearning, guilt about last argument before his death, persistent low mood, anhedonia, believes she should have died instead, avoiding reminders of husband, family saying 'it's been 10 months, get over it'
cases.risk_factors: Husband died suddenly of heart attack 10 months ago, unresolved conflict (last argument about money), no previous psychiatric history, children live abroad, social isolation since husband's death, cultural pressure to 'be strong'
cases.mse: Appearance: Appropriately dressed but appears grief-stricken. Behavior: Calm but emotionally distressed. Speech: Normal rate, tearful. Mood: 'I killed him with stress, I don't deserve to live'. Affect: Depressed, guilty. Thought: Preoccupation with husband, guilt about last argument, no suicidal ideation but says 'ready to join him'. Perception: No abnormality. Cognition: Intact. Insight: Partial - knows family wants her to recover but can't
cases.investigations: Blood: TSH normal, B12 normal, Hb slightly low. PHQ-9: 17/27 (moderate-severe). Normal grief typically improves 6-12 months post-loss
cases.suicide_risk: Moderate risk. Passive suicidal ideation ('join husband'), unresolved guilt is risk factor for complicated grief. Elderly female living alone
cases.explanation: Distinguishing normal grief from Major Depression: Grief is typically wave-like (mood improves temporarily), patient maintains self-esteem, thoughts often about deceased rather than self. Depression: persistent low mood, self-critical thoughts, functional impairment. Complicated Grief (Prolonged Grief Disorder) involves persistent, intense grief beyond expected duration (6+ months) with preoccupation, avoidance, etc. This case shows features of both complicated grief and depression, complicated by unresolved guilt about last argument. Cultural context: in Indian families, pressure to 'move on' may invalidate grief
cases.management: (1) Acknowledge and validate grief - distinguish from 'pathological' grief; (2) Complicated Grief Treatment (CGT) or grief-specific CBT; (3) Address guilt: work through last argument, rational reframe; (4) Explore continuing bonds (maintaining connection to husband while moving forward); (5) Family psychoeducation: grief takes time, pressure is counterproductive; (6) Consider medication if severe depression features; (7) Support group for widowed; (8) Address social isolation - community engagement; (9) Ritual completion (memorial, anniversary preparation); (10) If severe and prolonged, consider ECT; (11) Coordinate with community resources

cases.presenting_complaint: Gradually worsening low mood, fatigue, and cognitive problems over 4 months
cases.associated: Profound fatigue limiting daily activities, weight gain (6kg) despite reduced appetite, cold intolerance, dry skin and hair, constipation, cognitive complaints ('brain fog', poor memory), reduced libido, emotional blunting, menorrhagia
cases.risk_factors: Personal history of Hashimoto's thyroiditis (diagnosed 3 years ago, on levothyroxine but dose unchanged), recent dose decrease by GP (forgot to restart properly), no previous depression history
cases.mse: Appearance: Overweight, dry skin, thinning hair, slow movements. Behavior: Fatigued, slow to respond. Speech: Slow. Mood: 'Tired and sad'. Affect: Flat, restricted. Thought: Cognitive complaints but no specific negative cognitions. Perception: Normal. Cognition: Reports poor memory and concentration, MMSE normal. Insight: Good - suspects thyroid related
cases.investigations: Blood: TSH 28.5 mIU/L (markedly elevated), free T4 0.6 ng/dL (low), free T3 low-normal, TPO antibodies positive. PHQ-9: 14/27. Lipids: Elevated cholesterol and triglycerides. Ferritin low (iron stores depleted)
cases.suicide_risk: Low risk. No suicidal ideation, cognitive symptoms likely thyroid-related, good insight
cases.explanation: Hypothyroidism is a well-recognized cause of secondary depression, with prevalence of depressive symptoms in hypothyroid patients estimated at 30-50%. Symptoms overlap significantly: fatigue, cognitive impairment, sleep disturbance, appetite changes, emotional blunting. This patient has untreated hypothyroidism (likely from under-replacement) causing depressive symptoms. Improvement expected with adequate thyroid hormone replacement. Rule out: some patients develop depression despite 'normal' TSH (subclinical hypothyroidism with symptoms)
cases.management: (1) URGENT: Increase levothyroxine dose - typical increase 25-50mcg; (2) Recheck TSH in 6 weeks; (3) Expect depressive symptoms to improve over 4-8 weeks as euthyroidism restored; (4) May add SSRI temporarily if depression doesn't fully resolve with thyroid optimization; (5) Treat concurrent iron deficiency; (6) Monitor lipids; (7) Psychoeducation about thyroid-depression link; (8) Patient education about medication adherence; (9) Regular thyroid function monitoring; (10) If depression persists after euthyroidism achieved, treat as primary depression

cases.diagnosis: Depression in Context of Financial Crisis
cases.presenting_complaint: Low mood, sleep problems, and overwhelming stress following business failure and debt 3 months ago
cases.associated: Insomnia (difficulty falling asleep due to worry), reduced appetite, inability to concentrate on simple tasks, shame about failure, withdrawn from friends and family, guilt about not providing for family, passive death wishes ('my family would be better off if I wasn't a burden')
cases.risk_factors: Small business failed due to pandemic-related losses, substantial family debt, primary earner for family of 5, social stigma of business failure in community, wife working extra shifts, son had to leave private school, cultural pressure on men as providers
cases.mse: Appearance: Appropriately dressed but appears stressed and tired. Behavior: Restless, fidgety. Speech: Normal rate but talks excessively about financial problems. Mood: 'Shameful, I've failed everyone'. Affect: Anxious, depressed. Thought: Preoccupation with debt and failure, no active suicidal ideation but passive thoughts. Perception: No abnormality. Cognition: Poor concentration, otherwise intact. Insight: Good - recognizes depression but overwhelmed
cases.investigations: Blood: TSH normal, glucose normal (stress hyperglycemia possible). PHQ-9: 15/27. No substance use. Financial counseling assessment needed
cases.suicide_risk: Moderate-high risk. Male, financial crisis is major risk factor for suicide, passive SI, social isolation, cultural expectations of provider role. 'Failed provider' identity crisis
cases.explanation: Financial crisis and job loss are significant precipitants of depression, particularly in cultures where identity is closely tied to occupation and financial status. This patient shows adjustment disorder with depressed mood progressing to Major Depression. Risk factors: male sex (higher suicide rates), cultural expectations of male provider role, social isolation, shame and stigma preventing help-seeking. Financial stress compounds psychological stress. Social determinants of mental health are evident here
cases.management: (1) Assess and manage suicide risk; (2) SSRI for depression (e.g., sertraline 50-100mg); (3) Crisis counseling about debt and options; (4) Connect with financial counseling/debt relief services; (5) Address shame and cultural beliefs about failure; (6) Encourage social support - involve wife, trusted family/friends; (7) CBT for depression and financial stress; (8) Explore employment options (retraining, alternative work); (9) Address provider role beliefs; (10) Community support groups for business failure; (11) Follow-up weekly initially; (12) Consider local suicide prevention resources if high risk

cases.presenting_complaint: Persistent depression despite adequate trials of 3 different antidepressants over 18 months
cases.duration: Current episode: 18 months. History of depression: 12 years
cases.associated: Partial response to each medication but never remission, persistent low mood despite maximum doses, ongoing anhedonia, maintained job with difficulty, has tried therapy but 'doesn't help', side effects limiting doses (nausea, weight gain, sexual dysfunction), hopelessness about treatment
cases.risk_factors: Early onset depression (age 37), chronic relapsing course, family history of depression (mother, sister), childhood sexual abuse, multiple psychosocial stressors, personality traits (perfectionism, dependency)
cases.mse: Appearance: Well-groomed, resigned expression. Behavior: Cooperative but seems hopeless. Speech: Normal. Mood: 'Nothing works for me'. Affect: Mildly depressed, constricted. Thought: Hopeless about treatment, some passive SI but no plan. Perception: No abnormality. Cognition: Intact. Insight: Good - recognizes she has depression, frustrated by treatment resistance
cases.investigations: Blood: TSH normal, B12 normal, inflammatory markers slightly elevated (CRP 8). Trials documented with adequate dose and duration: (1) Sertraline 200mg x 8 weeks (partial response), (2) Venlafaxine XR 225mg x 10 weeks (partial response, nausea), (3) Escitalopram 20mg x 12 weeks (partial response, sexual dysfunction). PHQ-9: 14/27 (partial response to current treatment)
cases.suicide_risk: Moderate risk. Chronic illness, hopelessness, passive SI. Protective factors: intact social support, maintained function
cases.explanation: Treatment-Resistant Depression is defined as failure to respond to at least 2 adequate antidepressant trials. This patient meets criteria. TRD prevalence 30% of depressed patients. Contributing factors: genetic factors affecting drug metabolism, chronic stress, childhood trauma (alters HPA axis and neuroplasticity), inflammation, personality factors. Workup: check medication levels, thyroid, vitamin D, B12, consider inflammatory markers. Options: augmentation, combination, switching classes, ECT, ketamine, TMS, psychotherapy augmentation
cases.management: (1) Confirm TRD diagnosis - adequate trials documented; (2) Workup: CYP450 genotyping, vitamin D, inflammatory markers; (3) Augmentation strategies: add low-dose atypical antipsychotic (quetiapine, aripiprazole) or lithium or thyroid hormone; (4) Consider combination antidepressant (e.g., SSRI + bupropion for energy and sexual side effects); (5) Evaluate for ECT - highly effective for TRD (60-80% response); (6) Ketamine infusions (off-label, limited availability); (7) TMS if available; (8) Intensive psychotherapy (CBT, MBCT); (9) Address hopelessness - realistic hope; (10) Consider underlying trauma with EMDR or trauma-focused therapy; (11) Psychoeducation about chronic illness management; (12) Regular follow-up even if not fully remitted
